reviewMetadata.sourceLessonFamily: Reasoning with Linear Equations and Inequalities

learnerMaterial.title: Why the Inequality Sign Reverses
learnerMaterial.subject: mathematics
learnerMaterial.lessonGoal: Explain and apply the sign-reversal rule when solving a linear inequality.
successCriteria: I preserve the solution set at each step.
I reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
I verify a solution with a test value or graph.
keyPoints: An inequality compares order, not just equality.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses order.
A boundary check and test point can verify the result.

vocabulary.definition: all values that make a statement true

sections.title: Watch order reverse
sections.body: Start with 2 < 5. Multiply both sides by −1.

sections.title: Worked example: solve and verify
sections.directions: The answer and verification are shown.

steps: Divide by −3 and reverse the inequality: x ≥ −5.
Boundary check: x = −5 makes both sides equal.
Test x = 0: 4 ≤ 19 is true, and 0 is in x ≥ −5.
Therefore the solution set is x ≥ −5.

sections.title: Your turn: identify the critical move

feedback.correct: You divided by a negative number and reversed the order relation.
feedback.incorrect: The quotient is negative, and dividing by −4 reverses the inequality sign.

feedback.correct: Your algebra preserves the solution set, including the sign reversal on division.
feedback.incorrect: Subtract 7 first. When you divide the resulting inequality by −2, reverse the sign.

items.prompt: A student solves −6x < 24 and writes x < −4. Diagnose the error and give a test value that exposes it.

feedback.correct: You named the missing sign reversal and used substitution as evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Check what happens to order after division by −6. Then test a simple value such as 0 in the original statement.

sections.title: Reteach: compare two number-line images
sections.body: Multiplication by −1 reflects every point across 0. A point farther right becomes farther left, so the order reverses.

items.prompt: If a < b, which comparison is always true?

feedback.correct: You treated multiplication by −1 as a reflection that reverses order.
feedback.incorrect: Try a = 2 and b = 5, then compare −2 and −5 on a number line.

items.prompt: Solve 5 − 3(2x − 1) > 20. Justify the sign direction and verify with one value inside your solution set.

feedback.correct: Your symbolic steps, sign justification, and test value agree.
feedback.incorrect: Simplify first, isolate the negative x-term, and record exactly where division by a negative reverses the relation.

whatYouLearned: The inequality sign changes only when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
A test value checks whether the stated solution region is plausible.
